speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT AS TO PILOTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement on pilotage on the great lakes. There have been extensive consultations for scone time now between the interested departments and agencies in Canada and the United States on the subject of pilotage on the great lakes and adjacent waters. Emerging from these consultations has been an agreed method of how this problem could be handled. This method requires legislative concurrence in the two countries. The legislation need not, indeed cannot, be identical because of the differing constitutional structures in our two countries. Matching or parallel legislation, however, can be devised to meet the situation.
Legislation aimed at regulating pilotage in United States waters of the great lakes and St. Lawrence river has been introduced into the United States congress. That legislation, I understand, is being considered by the appropriate committee of the United States Senate today. An exchange of aide memoires took place last week. These aide memoires outline the areas of agreement reached during the consultations and state the intentions of the Canadian government with respect to its legislative proposals.
With the permission of the house I should like to have this exchange of aide memoires printed in Hansard. In addition I should like to have a supplementary exchange of letters referring to administrative action printed at the same time.

speechtext:
I have seen the article in question, Mr. Speaker. Our trade with Sweden is increasing, and I believe there are opportunities for Canadian exporters of materials and finished goods as well.
Canada's exports to Sweden in 1958 were about $11 million and in 1959 about $15 million, an increase of $4 million in the year. maintopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the adjournment of the house last evening I was speaking about the government's deficiency payments as applied to hogs and eggs. In my opening remarks last night I felt compelled to deny the allegations previously made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) to the effect that the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had indicated in a press conference on television last Tuesday that he was satisfied with the present system of deficiency payments. In support of my denial I should like at this time to put on record certain resolutions adopted at the last annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held in Toronto from January 26 to 28 last.
The first resolution with respect to eggs reads as follows:
Resolved that the Canadian government be asked to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act (by removing eggs from mandatory support, or alternatively by lowering the permissible level of mandatory support) so that offer to purchase support prices (for them) may be set at a suitable level.
The second resolution relating to eggs reads:
Resolved that an emergency floor price at a (non-incentive level) be established for eggs under the deficiency payment policy to protect the industry from further chaotic conditions.
With respect to hogs the federation passed the following resolution:
Resolved that the Canadian government be asked to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act by removing hogs from mandatory support, or alternatively by lowering the permissible level of mandatory support, so that offer to purchase support prices for them may be set at a suitable level.
A second resolution relating to this subject reads:
Resolved we strongly urge the federal government that some minimum offer to purchase support price on hogs be maintained in order to avoid a complete demoralization of the hog industry under the present deficiency payment policy.
I believe these resolutions clearly indicate the feeling of this important farm organization with regard to the present system of deficiency payments.
I should also like to refer at this time to certain remarks made in this house last night by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson). The hon. member, in referring to our criticisms of the system of deficiency payments on hogs and eggs, seemed to indicate that we were referring to a limited segment of Canadian agriculture only, and he then
1346	HOUSE OF
Disparity of National Income to Farmers proceeded to speak at length on policies affecting the grain growing industry in the western provinces.
Let me emphasize once again, Mr. Speaker, what we representatives of agricultural areas of the eastern provinces have often mentioned in this house. We do not object to any measure designed to assist the grain growers of the western provinces. We recognize that collectively the grain growing industry is the most important segment of Canadian agriculture. Nevertheless, let it be clearly understood that farmers in the eastern provinces and particularly those in the maritime provinces have a vital interest in certain forms of farm production other than grain growing. Eggs and hog production come under this category. Indeed, these smaller farm units to which I refer are the very lifeblood of many farm enterprises in the eastern provinces, and it is for this reason that we as representatives of these areas are deeply concerned with the deficiency payments now applying to eggs and hogs.
We are told that the object of the present system is to discourage these large integrated corporations and commercialized enterprises. Personally I am deeply disturbed at this view, for I question who will have to quit first, the small operator with limited capital or the large operator with almost unlimited resources.

I would now like to quote-

I shall now quote a few excerpts from the speech made in Victoria-ville by the chairman of the U.C.C. (Catholic farmers' union), Mr. Jean Baptiste Lemoyne, on December 20, 1959. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) has already referred to that document, but I think a record of such great significance bears repeating as often as possible.
After stating that farmers were walking in the fog towards the unknown, Mr. Lemoyne asked a few questions, and I quote:
Are we heading towards farm integration? Are we going to have a policy that will allow small farmers to survive? Is the family farm unit going to survive?


Our farming industry, he said, is still in a period of readjustment, and even today we wonder what is meant by an economically viable farm. Tomorrow's agriculture will be what those who guide its course will make it, i.e. we, the farmers, or those who process farm commodities, or those who control the marketing of food products. That is the great challenge we farmers have to face at this time.
It is obvious, he said, that the dislocations that have taken place in the farming industry started with the 1939 war. Because of the shortage of manpower, men had to be replaced by machines. The farmer was encouraged to produce more. Then too, he was shown modern methods of production. So it was that, one day, although we had barely noticed it, the farm industry had become completely transformed.
As for the government's deficiency payments program, that new policy seems to promote the multiplication of farm productions at a time when the trend is more or less mitigated specialization. There are many reasons why farmers should specialize: to cut down their investment in buildings, machinery and farm buildings and make better use of farm labour.
Mr. Lemoyne then pleads in favour of family farms, stating that in future the agricultural class will be either well organized and prosperous, or unorganized and hard up.
He said that the agricultural class needs leaders to ensure efficient and dynamic leadership within farm associations and other groups, such as cooperatives, etc.
The human factor with which we are now concerned should be given priority over economic and technical factors.
Can we accept a purely economic answer to the agricultural problem, disregarding the human values and social balance, represented by the farmer, who owns his property?
Could we find in an individual who is a member of a co-operative or collective farm, or in a labourer working for a large agricultural business, that innate prudence, that balance, that wisdom, that practical sense which have made the farmer known as a factor of balance and stability in our modem society.
It seems that on the family farm adapted to the needs of the time the farmer should be able to achieve the efficiency that can be expected from agricultural enterprise. All this depends primarily on the value of men who are cut out to be farmers and on the professional standards they will develop. The farmer is justified in demanding that the state provide research programs that would help determine the clashing forces and trends about which those who are responsible for leadership in agriculture are utterly in the dark.
This research should give special attention to the social problem of the farmer. We are already lagging behind in this respect, but better late than never. Acceptance of the fact that the answer to the farm problem is industrialization or "collectivization" of agriculture would be a public confession of our inability to take the lead and to act together on a professional level. If we really want to, we can preserve our type of family farm and enjoy a thriving agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to associate myself with those remarks that show such wisdom and forethought. I do not hesitate to draw the government's attention to this document, in which it could seek answers to the serious and complicated problems that face agriculture today.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it was most appropriate for the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). to have proposed a want of confidence motion having to do with support prices for agricultural commodities. I know, as he says, that in drafting a motion it would be difficult to state the No. 1 emergency problem facing the country. We have already succeeded in having a general debate concerning the unemployment situation. That being so, and recognizing the emergency agricultural situation, I think it was most appropriate that this amendment should be moved.
I would suggest that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has lifted the terms of his amendment from the preamble to Bill No. 237, to revise the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities, as passed by the House of Commons on January 25, 1958. In other words we in the opposition are in what I consider a very regrettable position, in that we are now able, with justification, to throw the terms of the government's own legislation into their teeth because they have failed to carry forward the terms of a statute which they themselves introduced and parliament subsequently passed.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) moved a subamendment asking that for hogs and eggs, support prices should be paid on various grades, and that consideration should be given to the question of deficiency payments on western grain.
I suggest that the government today is in trouble in many areas in this country. The government is in trouble so far as unemployment is concerned; the government is in trouble so far as agricultural prices are concerned. It is in trouble in some of its legislation with the government of the province of Manitoba, a Conservative government. It is in trouble with respect to another action with the government of the province of Ontario, so much so that a Conservative member of the Ontario legislature is reported to have threatened to resign if this government does not alter its course. And well this government might be in trouble, because it held up to the people of this country the promise of reform legislation, better days ahead, a correction of the errors of 22 years of Liberal administration.
Disparity of National Income to Farmers
Nowhere have people been more disappointed with the government than in the field of agriculture. Farmers had expected that this government meant what it promised; that when the Prime Minister, in the election campaigns, pointed out that he had on two separate occasions moved motions asking for parity prices for agriculture commodities he meant, as he said, to bring about this parity relationship.
Agricultural producers are tolerant people. They are patient people. They waited for the government to act. The government acted by presenting Bill No. 237, and from the terms of the bill and the statements of the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister agricultural producers expected that conditions would be better as a result of this legislation.
The government had not been returned to office with its tremendous majority a full year when organized agriculture became so disappointed with the government's failure to live up to its election commitments that a very large mass delegation was organized to come to Ottawa to ask for consideration of the grain farmers' problem.
It would not be fair to lay the entire blame for this situation at the doorstep of the government. As a matter of fact, when the delegation came to Ottawa and presented their brief on March 10 last year they pointed out on page 4 of the brief that the situation they were seeking to have corrected had been developing for many years. They said this:
In 1947 the farm price of wheat was at the reasonably satisfactory level of $1.63 per bushel. A decline occurred in the next few years, but this did not become too serious until 1953 when it dropped to $1.32. By the end of the marketing period for the 1956 crop, the price was down to $1.24.
That period was under the Liberal administration. On page 5 they went on to say:
During the same period that this decline in prices has occurred, farm costs have risen at a steady rate. The index of costs of goods and services used by farmers shows a rise in the period from 1947 to 1957 of 51.2 per cent. A further rise of 3.4 per cent above the 1947 level has occurred in 1958.
In other words, under Liberal administration from 1947 to 1957 there had been a drop in the price of wheat of 21 per cent and an increase in costs of 51 per cent. The delegation pointed out in their brief that in the following year, the first year of the present government's administration, there had been a further rise of 3.4 per cent in farm costs.
The delegation presented their brief on March 10. They were promised continuing consideration. The Prime Minister made a long speech to the delegation following their presentation, and he left them with the impression that action would be taken. But

Disparity of National Income to Farmers no action was taken, and so the delegation that presented a brief to the government on March 10 of last year had to interview the government once again on January 30 of this year, coming cap in hand and pointing out that they had been given the brush-off, that their brief had not been dealt with and that no decision had been made.
They pointed out something more. They pointed out in their second presentation that since March 10, 1958 there had been a further 4.1 per cent increase in the farm cost index, according to preliminary figures, and a 2.4 per cent increase in the price of wheat on the farm, so the net position has worsened in the last 11 months. In other words, according to preliminary figures the cost index in relation to 1947 is estimated at 159.2 per cent and the price of wheat is 80.9 per cent of what it was in 1947. After having organized this very large delegation; after having presented a comprehensive, well-documented brief to the government, and after having waited almost 11 months, the farmers report that in that intervening period their costs have risen by 4.1 per cent while the price of wheat has gone up by just 2.4 per cent.
The Prime Minister has not yet replied. He has not made a decision on the basis of that second request. But the delegation twisted the Prime Minister's arm. They said they wanted an early answer. They stated in their brief:
We therefore respectfully request the earliest possible decision of the government on this very urgent question, and if it happens that you are not prepared to give us your answer immediately, perhaps you would be prepared to advise us as to what date we may expect a reply.
It is a rather unheard of thing for a delegation meeting the Prime Minister to put before him a very positive request to make up his mind and, if he would not then, at least to give the delegation a date by which a decision would be made. After the delegation interviewed the Prime Minister he said that an answer would be given within 30 days. If an answer is given within 30 days it will be almost exactly 12 months from the time the delegation first arrived in Ottawa and presented its case to the government.
This delegation came from the prairies. It represented the people of the prairies who did more than their share in supporting and electing this government. This delegation represents the people of Saskatchewan, the people of Alberta and Manitoba who supported the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. After having shown such

great confidence in the government they have nevertheless been given a slap in the face by a government that has refused for almost a full year even to have the courtesy to give them a full reply to their excellent brief.
Since the committee representing the original farm delegation and the people of the prairies presented their brief to the government, the interprovincial farm union council also presented a brief on February 7, and in their brief they point out how conditions have been worsening under the present administration. I quote from page 3:
The disparity between farm prices and costs in Canada is continuing to widen. The October, 1959, national index for prices of farm products stood at 235.9 and represented a decline of 6.1 points from the 1958 annual average of 242. The composite national index for commodities and services used by farmers, exclusive of living component, for August, 1959, stood at 272, up 14.5 points from the 1958 national average of 257.5. The November, 1959 issue of The Current Review predicts that the trend toward increased farm costs is expected to continue into 1960 while farm income will remain stable or decline, resulting in declines for both realized farm net income and farm net income in I960.
In other words, since the prices stabilization act was passed conditions for the agricultural producers of this country have worsened. Their costs have gone up, and this index shows that the price-cost squeeze is even worse now than it was a year ago.
Agricultural producers expected this government to act. They had a lot of confidence in Bill No. 237. Spokesmen and candidates supporting the government party went back and forth across this country saying, "You asked us to provide adequate support prices for agricultural products, and we have done so". They said, "We have placed absolute floors under nine key commodities. Not only have we placed absolute floors under these key commodities, but we are placing these floors on a precise formula. This is your guarantee. This is your Magna Carta. This will enable you to farm and plan your production with a degree of certainty you have never had before". Those were fine words, and much was expected.
But, Mr. Speaker, the administration and interpretation of the act has destroyed the promises contained in those fine sounding words. The government has decided against providing floor prices by means of an offer to buy a product at the floor price. The government, instead, is following a policy of allowing the market to take its course, of attempting to determine national averages for a period in advance or set them for a period in advance and then using the deficiency payment technique to pay producers certain sums of money if they do not get

Disparity of National Income to Farmers
that average price in the market. The government has decided to limit the amount of production on which such deficiency payments can be made.
I have checked the debates on this legislation and I have checked the speeches that were made by members of the government prior to the 1958 election. I can find no instance where these spokesmen said that the 80 per cent of the base price would apply to only a portion of the production of Canadian farms. No mention at all was made during the debate of any limit. One can look through the bill, and there is no mention of the 80 per cent being paid only on a limited quantity of agricultural products. I have in my hand a copy of the bill as passed by the House of Commons, and on page 2, paragraph (e) of subclause 1 of clause 1 I find this:
"prescribed price" means,
(i) in relation to a named commodity, 80 per cent of the base price thereof, or such higher percentage of the base price thereof as the governor in council prescribes-
Producers were led to believe that the 80 per cent would apply to the nine agricultural commodities, and were never informed that it would apply to only a certain quantity from each farm. I protested this provision last year; not because there should not be perhaps some limitation, but I felt that the government itself was breaking the law as passed by parliament by placing limitations on the price supports as provided in the act.
There are other sections of this act, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that are not being fulfilled by the government. In other words the government is flouting a law of this parliament and is failing to implement what is legally required by law. Clause 8 of the bill, now section 8 of the act, reads as follows:
In each year the board shall establish the base price for each agricultural commodity, or the grade, quality, variety, class, type or form thereof, the price of which is to be stabilized under this act.
I point out that there is no suggestion that there shall be a limit on the quantity. There may be differences as to the grade, quality, variety, class, type or form thereof, but no mention is made of limitation on quantity. Subsection 2 of the same section read's as follows:
The base price of an agricultural commodity shall be the average price at representative markets as determined by the board for the 10 years immediately preceding the year in which the base price is established.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker:
The base price of an agricultural commodity shall be the average price at representative markets as determined by the board for the 10 years-
This section of the act has not been fulfilled. There is no guaranteed base price at representative market points. Instead, the government have taken what they call a national average which does not take into account the variations in market prices over the 10-year period at representative marketing points. The government's failure to fulfill this part of the act is one of the main reasons they are running into such great criticism in the country. This means that under this act people who are away from the main marketing centres will get much less for their products than had they been guaranteed 80 per cent of the base price at representative markets.
The government has not provided a floor price, a minimum price even, on the best grades which it alleges it is supporting under this act. The national average of 33 cents a dozen for grade A large eggs is declared to be the price for the purpose of calculating deficiency payments over a three-month period. It is possible, and it will certainly happen, that a very large quantity of the eggs that are sold at less than 80 per cent of the base price will have no deficiency payments made on them whatever; because if the price goes above the national average, then to the extent that the price goes above the national average in those three months it destroys the chances of a farmer who is receiving less than the national average.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government is denying payments under this act that they are required by law to make. I suggest that the government, in fact, is stealing money that legitimately belongs to the producers under the terms of this legislation.

Disparity of National Income to Farmers producers of moneys that, in my opinion, they are required by law to give the producers. The government are breaking their own law. The government are breaking the terms of this statute which was passed by the House of Commons in good faith and in clear terms. The act says that the government will provide support prices at 80 per cent of the base price at representative marketing points. This has not been done, and this is not being done. This act as it is being interpreted by the government has been made a phony act apparently because the government's promises have been phony, and the legislation is part and parcel of the window dressing that has taken place by a phony government as far as its promises are concerned or as far as the implementing of this statute is concerned.
The government has said that this support will be limited to certain grades. Because the government is limiting this to certain grades-grade A large eggs, shall we say, for example-and because the government has failed to provide minimum prices but instead lets the market take its course, this means a low price for grade A large eggs, depressed prices for grade A medium eggs which have no semblance of support whatsoever and depressed prices for grade B eggs; and in fact deprives the producers of grade A medium eggs and grade B eggs of support that should have flowed from the fulfillment of this act. The government is depressing the market by its action. It is destroying hundreds of egg producers in this country, and it is discriminating as between regions.

That is what this legislation is doing. This is what it has done. One does not have to take my word for it. Perhaps the hon. gentleman opposite would be more impressed by the words of Hon. George Hutton, the minister of agriculture in the government of the province of Manitoba, a Conservative government. He was so greatly disturbed about the government's egg program that, in the Manitoba legislature, he read a letter he had sent to the federal Minister of Agriculture -a Conservative colleague if you will-outlining his fears about this act. From the Winnipeg Free Press of February 16, page 1, I read as follows:
The provincial Conservative government has warned the federal Conservative government that it views "with very great alarm" the effect of federal government's policy on deficiency payment for eggs. A provincial protest on the egg policy was read to the legislature Monday night by Hon. George Hutton.

He was reading from a letter he had sent to the federal minister.
The letter began:	"The Manitoba government
views with very great alarm the effect of the deficiency payment policy in respect to eggs implemented by your agriculture stabilization board a few weeks ago."
The policy placed Manitoba farmers in "an untenable position" and made them face an intolerable situation," Mr. Hutton said.
That is strong language.
He said that Manitoba was a surplus producing area in eggs. Producers were a thousand miles away from deficiency areas. There was regularly a 3 to 4 cent difference between Winnipeg and Montreal quotations on grade A large.
There is much more that follows, Mr. Speaker, but it is all in the same vein, pointing out the disturbing aspects of this policy.

I had said, when this legislation was under discussion in the house originally, that there was no intention that this support price would not be paid, that there were basic minimums below which prices would not be allowed to fall; because at page 2188 of Hansard of December 11, 1957 the Minister of Agriculture himself made this statement:
In addition to the flexible guaranteed prices which may be applied to any agricultural commodity and which will be the ones in general use, the legislation provides for that sense of security which farmers have asked for and which we believe they are entitled to by providing assured floor prices-
I direct attention to the words "floor prices".
-for certain key commodities.
There is no floor price on eggs and there is no floor price on hogs. This is done by writing into the legislation a provision that those commodities must be supported under any circumstances at 80 per cent of the base price. It is not expected that these will be the guaranteed prices in effect. The guaranteed prices will be higher in most cases. But this provision is written into the legislation so the farmer will be absolutely assured that no matter how prices may slide, he will at the very least receive 80 per cent of the base price.
That statement is not being followed. Floor prices do not exist. By failing to provide base prices at representative marketing points and by failing to provide floor prices the government is denying agricultural producers part of the money to which they are entitled, in my opinion, under this act for the grades that are supported, to say nothing of the
further sums of money of which they are deprived for grades that are not supported.
This legislation, as it has been interpreted and as it is being implemented, is damaging the agricultural industry. It is a great disappointment to the agricultural producers and, in my submission, the government itself is failing to fulfil the law as set forth in this act.
The Minister of Agriculture says the reason he is providing a system of deficiency payments is that production will be reduced. That was no part of the discussion of the former legislation. The legislation which was formerly discussed was placed before the house, according to the minister, to guarantee floor prices, support prices. Now he deliberately says that the purpose of this policy is to reduce production, to force farmers to curtail the production they have been providing in the last one-year period.
We have a surplus today of some agricultural products but I do not think, in terms of the needs of the people of Canada or in terms of the needs of the people of the world, that we should view these surpluses with alarm, or that we should take precipitate action to damage the production of agricultural producers or to bring the prices of agricultural commodities to the lowest price since the thirties.
We should be taking action in international trade to see that surplus food products reach people who are hungry and who need surplus food. The Russians are today boasting that by 1965 their agricultural production will exceed that of the United States. If the Soviet union's production exceeds that of the United States, does anybody here think they will say there is a tremendous surplus and they are going to curtail production? No; they will continue their economic offensive to undermine Canadian markets, Canadian agriculture and the democratic form of government. I suggest to the minister that the issue of maintaining agricultural production transcends the needs of Canada itself, because food production and greater food production is essential to the survival of the democratic form of government in the world.
I listened to the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Brunsden) yesterday with a good deal of interest. I disagree with most of what he said. He talked about hogs and eggs being in and out products. I think we are facing today an in and out government. It came in very quickly and apparently very easily, and if it does not alter this and other policies it will be defeated just as quickly as it was elected.

Mr. Speaker, I was unable to be here yesterday, as I had to attend a large and important agricultural function in Alberta in honour of the last year's world wheat king, a young man named Douglas Mackintosh, who won the world wheat championship at the age of 18, a very notable achievement.
The fact that it was fairly well advertised that I was going to be at this affair yesterday had, I hope, no significance with regard to the timing of this particular motion. It certainly was a disappointment to me that I was not here for the discussion yesterday, and it was rather difficult as far as this particular function was concerned, because I had to leave practically as soon as it had started in order to get a plane to be back here today. As a result of sitting up all night in the plane without much sleep I am not at my brightest today; but in view of the criticisms I have been able to read so far I do not have to be at my brightest in order to answer them.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read again the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), because the amendment is in practically the same terms as those contained in the preamble to the stabilization act. It is as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the government should give immediate consideration to the implementation of agricultural policies designed for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that this is an amendment which constitutes a sort of trick motion. We as a government have been exerting every effort to do, and actually doing, what the motion says we should consider doing. I think I can establish later in my remarks that we have had considerable success in moving toward the goal set out in the preamble to the Agricultural Stabilization Act which is recited again in this motion. All the numerous policies we have initiated, all the great volume of agricultural legislation we have introduced into this house, have been directed toward the very end set out in this motion, which is also set out, as I say, in the preamble to the stabilization act.
I would ask, Your Honour and hon. members of this house, and any person in the country, to compare what we have actually done as a government in the last two and three quarter years, approximately now, to assist agriculture with the almost complete inactivity of the Liberal government in this

regard during the last 10 years it was in office. All that is necessary to demonstrate the really completely impossible position of the Liberal party as far as agriculture is concerned is to look at that record, and that is all I ask anybody to do. There is complete proof in that record of the efforts we have since made to attain the goal set forth in the preamble to the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
In considering agricultural matters at the present time the most important fact we have to keep in mind is that the great technological revolution in agriculture has been going on now for some very considerable length of time. It has been in operation for at least the last 40 years, but it has greatly speeded up during the last 20 years. It has created entirely new conditions which require new thinking, new approaches and new policies if the new situations which have arisen as a result of this technological revolution are to be met successfully, or if there is to be any hope of meeting them successfully. We have recognized that this is the situation, and we have demonstrated it by the numerous new policies we have put into effect and which we think have a very good chance of solving the agricultural problems which have existed in this country now for many years past.
The Liberal party, on the contrary, still seem to be living in the past. They appear to think that what was good enough 15 years ago is good enough today. They refused, Mr. Speaker, to put into effect an adequate price support program. They refused improved credit facilities which were urgently needed. They refused to put into effect crop insurance. They refused to put into effect cash advances on farm-stored grain. They refused to give any financial assistance in respect to crops which were snowed under in the years 1951 and 1952. They refused so many things that it would take me the rest of the 40 minutes I am allowed in order to list them.
In other words, particularly during the last 10 years they were in office they refused practically everything as far as agriculture was concerned. Now they attack this present government because we have initiated new policies which are adapted to the realities of the situation which actually exists at the present time.
The technological revolution in agriculture to which I have referred has had two great effects. It has caused a very large drop in the number of farmers and a great increase in the amount of production. From those two facts, of course, have flowed extremely important results from the marketing point

of view, the production point of view, the social point of view and from every point of view that affects agriculture and in all the ways that this industry affects the economy as a whole.
From 1941 to 1958 the number of farmers in Canada has been reduced from 677,000 to 555,000, a reduction of 17 per cent. The figures I have given represent merely the reduction in the number of farms in Canada. The reduction in the farm labour force has been very much greater. During the period when this large reduction in the number of farms and in the farm labour force was taking place there was a marked increase in the volume of production. I am not referring to the dollar value of production which of course has increased tremendously. The volume of production increased from 1941 to 1958 by 27 per cent. I think even more important than that, this production could have been increased by more than that if there had been any reasonable possibility of the farmers marketing that production.
I believe we must recognize that this outstanding fact has created a completely new situation in agriculture and particularly as far as marketing is concerned.
I do wish that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), to whose remarks in this debate I am about to refer, would continue their conversation out behind the curtain. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River directed a great deal of his speech to the hog and egg situation. The basic fact in the hog and egg situation which seems to have completely escaped the hon. gentleman is that the technological revolution has made it possible to produce almost unlimited quantities of eggs, poultry meat and hogs. The only limit on the production of these commodities at the present time is the amount of cereal grains available in Canada for feeding poultry and hogs. We all know that we have a very large volume of cereal grains available. If the prices of eggs and hogs were up materially, within two years we could be producing in Canada probably three times our present egg production and probably twice as many hogs without any difficulty at all. In other words, the possibilities of production of these particular commodities on a factory line basis of production particularly are almost unlimited.
At the present time as far as egg production is concerned a man does not even have to have a farm because it is not essentially a farming operation but is a factory operation. A man may have an acre or two of land and a three or four storey building and he can have thousands of hens laying eggs in his egg factory. That is what it is, in
Disparity of National Income to Farmers essence. The feed is taken in mechanically, the eggs are collected mechanically and so forth. This is not a farming operation in the real sense of the word.
This type of factory production is also going on extensively as far as poultry meat is concerned. It was also starting in hog production. It was quite evident that under those circumstances it would be completely impossible to market an almost unlimited production such as was possible with these new methods. The production was not even being accomplished by farmers but was to a large extent operated by people who were not farmers and who had other occupations. They could see that there was money in this type of operation and so they financed and set up operations of that nature. It was these people who were largely responsible for the surplus production of eggs and hogs. As long as the government stood ready to purchase every pound of pork and every egg produced it was quite evident that this situation which started as far back as 1954 and increased year by year would continue to increase more rapidly until an impasse was created.
It was quite apparent, therefore, that the system of support by means of purchase had to be changed. There was no alternative to that at all. The existing system was completely unrealistic. It was completely contrary to the tenor of the Agricultural Stabilization Act to have the government pay out the taxpayers' money for the support of people who were essentially not farmers at all and who as a result of their factory-type production were driving many average farmers out of production. That is the basic reason why it is no longer possible to continue support by means of purchase a method which hon. members opposite by their arguments seem to insist we should continue to employ. Such a method is no longer possible in relation to these two products or any other commodities where surpluses can develop once operators institute factory-line methods of production.

The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River went on after that to ask, was it our intention to depart completely from the purchase method. He stated at page 1301 of Hansard:
There is every reason to inquire whether or not there is an intention to depart completely from this offer to purchase system.
When the Agricultural Stabilization Act was passed and I think in every speech I made on this subject subsequently in this house and outside, it was to the effect that the act provided for various methods of support. It is necessary, in any reasonable system, to have various methods to support the price. One of these methods is purchase, and we are still using it and under certain circumstances and for certain products it is the best method to use. Then there is the deficiency payments method of support which we are using for a considerable number of products. There is the flat payment method which we have used for some products. Any other method which it is found desirable to use can be used under the stabilization act; that is part of its essential flexibility.
All of these methods are being used and will be used. There is no intention of dropping any one of them. Which method will be used depends upon the commodity, what the circumstances are at the time and particularly whether it will produce the best result for the greatest number of average farmers in Canada. That is what we are striving to do under the stabilization act.
The next thing I should like to mention is found down at the bottom of this same page, namely page 1301. The hon. member tried to make out that the difficulties that arose as to surpluses were due to the fact that we had set incorrect prices. As reported at page 1301 of Hansard he said this:
If it has proven unsatisfactory-
That is the method of purchase.

It has been established that they did set what they were warned not to do, namely incentive prices. It was not the system that was at fault, it was the decisions made by this government.
Mr. Speaker, this is completely contrary to what the hon. member was arguing to
Disparity of National Income to Farmers begin with, to what the resolution states and to all his previous argument which was to the effect that we had set prices too low. This has been the position of the Liberal party throughout. At the time the stabilization act was put into effect they were complaining that we were going to set prices too low; and when we did set prices, they said they were set too low.
In the election of 1958, after the act had been passed, the Leader of the Opposition was going around the country saying that the price of 58 cents for butter was too low, that it should be 63 cents, and the same thing with regard to other commodities. At this time they said the price was too low, that we should set it up higher. Then, in the debate on the speech from the throne the Leader of the Opposition was arguing that we had set prices too high.
They have no policy with regard to this matter. They have no consistency whatever with regard to the matter. Here is the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in the same speech, in the first part of it condemning us because we set prices too low and because we are not giving the farmers a fair share of the national income. Now in this later part of his speech he is condemning us because we set prices too high. I leave it to anybody who reads his speech to conclude whether he is reasonable in his remarks and whether he has not completely contradicted his first position by the second one he has taken in this section I have just dealt with.
However, I may say that when we were setting these prices immediately after the stabilization act was passed nobody advised any lower prices. All the advice we received was for higher prices. In spite of what the hon. member says about farm organization, not one farm organization at that time asked for any lower prices. It is true that shortly after I had announced that the deficiency payment method of support would go into effect for hogs and eggs some of them said, "We should set lower support prices". But up until that time they all wanted higher support prices; that is, of course, higher support prices by means of purchase.
The next matter to which I should like to refer is this. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, as reported at page 1301 of Hansard, stated:
they have created complete chaos in this country with respect to the production of both eggs and hogs.
The figures I have shown with regard to hog prices and the figures I have quoted with regard to the way in which egg prices are already improving demonstrate, in my opinion, quite conclusively that there has been no such thing as chaos in prices. There

Disparity of National Income to Farmers has been a necessary readjustment taking place in the price structure which will accomplish the purpose of bringing production down into line with what can be marketed.
I think those are all the points I need to mention in that speech. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), as reported at page 1307 of Hansard, moved a subamendment that these words be inserted:
-which will include consideration of support prices for various grades of hogs and eggs and the consideration of deficiency payments on grain

I am not going to say anything about the latter point. In fact, I note that I have not time in which to do so. But as to putting into effect deficiency payments for all grades of commodities, by doing that what you would be doing in effect would be subsidizing low quality production, the very thing which we have been trying to get away from by paying premiums with regard to hogs for example.
I do not think any good agriculturist in this country, a purebred breeder, anybody at an agricultural college or any good farmer would say that we should pay deficiency payments on-in other words subsidize from the treasury-low grade production. We must produce constantly better and better products in this country if we are going to have any hope of expanding our markets either at home or abroad. To pay deficiency payments for grade B eggs or grade C and grade D hogs would merely be to perpetuate the production of low quality products and I think it would be completely unjustified to use taxpayers' money for that purpose.
I have mentioned the fact that the hon. member for Assiniboia made the same sort of statement as that made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, namely that since the stabilization act was passed the condition of the farmers has worsened. I have demonstrated twice now, I think, that such is not the case but that the contrary, it has been improved since the stabilization act was passed. I should like to say that this constant reiteration of statements which are demonstrably incorrect not only proves nothing but merely wastes the time of this house and, of course, it shows the unreliability of the statements of persons who say things of that kind. In addition, I think it does them damage as far as the country generally is concerned.

We say that the government, by its own repudiation, has gone back not only on its own policies but on its own assurances. We were reminded yesterday by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) of the observation of the Prime Minister, parity, not charity. We recall the strong declarations made by the present Minister of Agriculture and the demands that he made when he sat in opposition to the previous administration. We recall particularly the words of the Prime Minister uttered in 1957 and already referred to by my colleague, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. Listen to them. The Prime Minister said:
We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income by maintaining a flexible, and I underline the word "flexible", price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers based on a fair price-cost relationship.
Note that, "a fair price-cost relationship". That statement contained three promises; first, the assurance of a fair share of the
Disparity of National Income to Farmers national income; second, an adequate parity; and, third, a fair price-cost relationship. All of these were to be received and guaranteed through a flexible price support program. These words were uttered in 1957. The Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister before the election of 1958 assured the house that the farmers would receive guaranteed yearly prices so that, as the Prime Minister put it-these words are significant-the farmer may know in anticipation each year what he is going to receive. The objective of guaranteed yearly prices, the Prime Minister said, was to give the farmer a fair share of the national income.
What is the situation today? I listened to the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, both of whom in some particulars directed against the administration an argument that I believe is incontestable because the government, in violation of its promises, has substituted a deficiency payment program for payments to the producers of two important agricultural commodities, eggs and hogs. They have forgotten altogether both what the act says and what they promised, namely guaranteed yearly prices.
The minister spoke a while ago and said that what would happen with regard to these two commodities was happening now with regard to the application of price supports on soya beans. The minister knows perfectly well that what is done with soya beans is an averaging on the national price and while the floor is designated as $2 the farmer never does know in advance, because of this averaging process, what price he will receive for that particular commodity any more than the egg producer or hog producer will know under this deficiency payment program.

In the first place, the so-called support price should be increased to take into account the rising cost of production. At present, the support price is recommended by the board and approved by the government. It is at the mandatory or emergency level, and is not related in any way to the upward trend of production costs. However, the board is obliged by the present legislation to maintain a fair relationship between the price received by the farmer and his costs. For instance, the support price which otherwise would be prescribed in each given year could be adjusted to take care of the change in costs which occurred during the previous year. I am sure that the board, in consultation with farm organizations, could devise other and perhaps more suitable formulae.
Our second proposal is to urge that the government introduce regional average market prices in the calculation of deficiency payments. The minister has already rejected this on the ground that if regional market prices were used, regional support prices would also have to be used and nobody would be better off. This it seems to me is a poor argument. When prices for the same commodity vary from one region to another, a national system of deficiency payments discriminates against those regions where prices are low and which, therefore, need more
Disparity of National Income to Farmers assistance, and in favour of those regions where prices are higher and which, therefore, need less assistance. Indeed, a uniform national deficiency payment may not be enough to bring the prices received by producers in the less conveniently located regions up to the national average prices or up to the support prices, but it will be a windfall return for those producers located in regions where the market price is already above the national average or support price.
Such a result is undesirable. After all, a deficiency payment is a government subsidy designed to correct the deficiencies of market mechanisms and it is only normal that, so far as practicable, those producers who are in a less favourable position in the marketplace should receive proportionately more than others who have already got price support on the ordinary market.
For all these reasons, I submit that deficiency payments, if that is the policy which the government proposes to continue to pursue, should be calculated as the difference between the national support price and the average regional market price. Such graduated deficiency payments would not complicate the administration of the scheme. They would be fairer than the present system and in greater conformity with the requirements of our legislation. If that is the policy the government wishes to pursue, then we offer this as a better way of embarking upon a policy which we contend is a repudiation of the government's own program.

The price stabilization act, Mr. Speaker, is applied by means of a revolving fund of $250 million. Young farmers, from 21 to 45 years old, are thus able to set up their farm on an altogether sound basis. The loan ceiling can be as high as 75 per cent of the assessed value of the farm, including equipment and livestock, up to a maximum of $27,500. Moreover, the government has set the interest rate for those loans at 5 per cent.
