speechtext: It is a matter that you are bringing to the attention of the public.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friends will allow me to pursue my statement for a moment before they begin to interrupt. We get a great deal of interruption in this house but interrupting before a speech has begun is something new in parliament. Whatever

Crisis in Uranium Industry hon. members who have already interrupted may think, this is a matter which concerns not only those workers who will be jobless because of what is happening to this industry but it is a matter of great national importance because it concerns an export trade which this year, according to the official figures, will be something over $300 million-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: -an export trade which, to say the least, is in jeopardy.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
If my hon. friends can recover from their postprandial exuberance I will continue my remarks.
The centre of this industry, the place where the greatest production takes place, is in and around the new modern community of Elliot Lake. Indeed, I think about 70 per cent of the uranium produced at the present time comes from that area.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: In your constituency.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Indeed it is in my constituency in which I have managed to get elected five times. My hon. friend would be lucky if he had an equally good constituency.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Order. I hope that my hon. and exuberant friends will restrain themselves and give the Leader of the Opposition an opportunity to make his point.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I echo your hope, Mr. Speaker, although from past experience I cannot say that I share it.
This community of Elliot Lake, which has now developed into a thriving modern town of between 25,000 and 27,000 people, sees its future in jeopardy because of what has happened to the uranium industry. In that community of Elliot Lake the federal government and the provincial government of Ontario have put something between $50 million and $70 million in order to aid in the development of that city. It would be-and I am sure all members will agree-a matter of the greatest possible importance and the greatest possible distress not only to the community but to all Canadians if this city were to become a ghost town. I just mentioned the importance of the industry. The trade figures show how important it is. It is important also to find out how this industry got into the situation in which it finds itself at the present time.
This matter of responsibility must be of great importance because the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), instead of replying to questions which were

addressed to him on this subject, has always managed to make some political allusion to the responsibility for the situation in which the industry finds itself. Therefore it is necessary to deal with that matter and I intend to do so. I intend to take the time which is necessary, including interruptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Will you give me a chance to reply?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I intend to make my speech. The hon. minister who is now asking for the right to reply and his colleagues are about the last men in this house to complain about someone getting up and making a speech, and not allowing a reply to be made. That, of course, is their favourite tactic, but when it is used against them they do not like it.
As hon. members know, at least as those who know anything about this matter know, the production of uranium in this country goes to the United States of America with the exception of a relatively small amount which goes to the United Kingdom and even smaller amounts which go to other countries. Our export of uranium to the United States has been covered by a contract made by agencies of the two governments. It was a five-year contract which included in its terms options which could be taken up by the United States government before the expiry of the contract, which I think was in 1962.
It is interesting in this regard-no doubt the minister most concerned will be aware of this-to recall the circumstances which existed at the time of the negotiation of this contract and at the time of the signing of the agreement. At that time, from 1953 on, when we were talking about a contract of this kind, so far as this important commodity was concerned we were in a situation of scarcity, not of surplus. It was a situation of dangerous scarcity for an essential defence material, the scarcity of which at that time and for some time after these negotiations began was the cause of very great anxiety to all those concerned with the defence of the western world.
Very great pressure was brought to bear at that time on Canadian authorities to take every possible step to increase production as quickly as possible of this essential war material. Nevertheless, though that pressure was great, though the need was great and the importance was great, there was some question in the minds of those concerned with this matter in government as to whether we should in those circumstances have tied up all the production of uranium in this country, or almost all of it, in one contract, let alone a contract which was for five years. There was certainly no suggestion at that time in

anybody's mind that we should tie up our complete production of this very scarce material for a period beyond five years.
It is interesting, in reading the discussion which took place in the committee of the house concerned with energy questions, and in the house itself, to recall that in all of those discussions there was not a single occasion when any member of the opposition of that day, including the present Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), suggested there was anything wrong with this contract in regard to its term. The only suggestion made by the opposition of the day was whether we would get enough uranium and were sufficiently aware of the danger of the scarcity of this commodity in the world.
Perhaps I can quote from the leader of the opposition at that time, Mr. George Drew, as repored at page 6441 of Hansard for July 20, 1955, who was replying to a statement made by the minister of trade and commerce at that time, Mr. C. D. Howe. Mr. Drew said:
Mr. Speaker, X have no desire to pursue this unnecessarily beyond the extreme importance of this development.
This was the contract. He went on:
Is it not true that the opinion has been expressed that, with the peacetime developments of the use of uranium, it is unlikely that the supply will keep pace with demand?
That is what was worrying the opposition at that time, including some of the hon. gentlemen sitting opposite me now who are trying to create the impression that what we should have done, as those responsible for this contract, was to tie up our total production for a period of longer than five years.
The same fear that we might run out of this material existed both in the United States and the United Kingdom. If hon. members read The Economist, the current edition for February 13, at page 639 they would come across a paragraph which gives the feeling which existed in the United Kingdom at the time this contract was signed. This paragraph reads as follows:
When that program-
That is the United Kingdom program for the development of nuclear energy.
-was first drafted, experts foresaw two possible threats to its fulfilment: that industry might not be able to tackle the vast building program, and that world production of natural uranium might not be sufficient to meet the fuel needs of a nuclear power program of this size.
In the United Kingdom they were also worried whether there would be enough uranium to go round, and they were the more worried because of the contract we had made with the United States, which had to be modified in order to make uranium
Crisis in Uranium Industry available for United Kingdom needs. Indeed, there were many other authorities at that time who had the same worries about this scarcity of uranium.
As I have said, members of the government when in opposition had no word of caution or criticism at that time about this five-year contract. The only thing which worried them, as far as I can gather from the record, was whether we were wise in tying up our supply with the United States for five years, and whether we had sufficiently taken into account the possibility of a scarcity of uranium. Even as late as October 1957 the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) had the same feeling about the uranium situation. He certainly had no worry at that time about what might happen to the uranium industry of this country because of over-supply. In speaking to the transportation club of Ottawa on October 10, 1957, he said, and I am quoting from his speech:
Just a few weeks ago we had the official opening of the world's largest uranium mine in the Blind River area of northern Ontario.
As we enter the atomic age and nuclear industrial power becomes a reality, production of uranium will assume increasing importance in the Canadian economy. The industrial development of nuclear power on this continent, in Europe and elsewhere is creating a demand for uranium of such magnitude-
I repeat, this is the Minister of Transport speaking as a member of the government in October 1957.
that we can now look forward to continued and extensive development in this phase of the mining industry.
Was the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself very worried about the situation two years ago? Was he planning what might happen when this contract expired if effective steps were not taken with the United States government to have the United States government take up the option? Were he and his colleagues bringing the kind of political pressure to bear on the United States government which was essential if these options were to be taken up in whole or in part? What was his reaction when he was pressed by the opposition in this house about those difficulties and dangers and worse that would occur if action were not taken by the government to see that the United States lived up to its moral obligation to take up some of these options, if not all of them? The hon. gentleman was continually pressed by hon. members on this side of the house who were aware of what might happen, if the government was not aware of its own responsibilities.
On April 14, 1959, as recorded at page 2657 of Hansard, I addressed a question to the minister about his talks in Washington. In reply the minister referred to his one day

Crisis in Uranium Industry visit to Washington which was the only visit he had on this question so far as I know. We were worried about what would happen if these talks were not successful. This is what the minister said:
This is the first opportunity X have had to meet with him-
That refers to Mr. McCone, head of the United States atomic energy commission. The minister continued:
-and with other members of the commission. We discussed matters of general interest with regard to the atomic energy program affecting our two countries.
The minister said that this was the first opportunity there was to discuss matters affecting an industry of such vital importance in Canada. He went on to say:
Further conversations with respect to the particular matter raised by the Leader of the Opposition will be held in the near future.
Since that time we have been trying to get some information about these further conversations but without any success at all.
A few days later on April 20, 1959, as reported at page 2835 of Hansard, I asked the Prime Minister whether he would comment on a statement made from Washington immediately after the Minister of Trade and Commerce had left Washington to the effect that United States uranium imports from Canada would be cut down by more than two thirds after June 30, 1962. That was a statement by a United States official concerned with atomic energy matters in the United States made in that country right after the minister had been there. If that was not a warning as to what might happen if steps were not taken, I do not know what more drastic warning one could get. In reply to that question the Prime Minister said:
I realize the situation in general with regard to uranium, as I am sure the hon. gentleman does, and also the difficulties which lie ahead. By 1962 we trust that steps will be taken in order to meet the needs of the two countries, and that agreements will be arrived at.
That was the statement of the Prime Minister which did not indicate any great worry about this situation. I was not satisfied, of course, with that kind of reaction from the government, especially in the light of the reports we were getting from Washington as to what was going to happen. I point out that these were public statements. On April 21, 1959 I again brought up the matter in the house as reported at page 2913 of Hansard of that date. This is the question I asked having regard to what I considered to be the cavalier treatment accorded to our minister by the authorities in Washington concerned with this matter when he visited that city. I said:

To say the least, that is a discourteous way to treat a Canadian minister to make such a statement, only a few days after he had been down to Washington.
I referred, of course, to the statement to the effect that the United States was going to cut off this contract. I went on to say:
I hope to impress upon the United States government, not only the importance of this export trade but also the fact that the United States government has a moral duty to take up those contracts, because it was not many years ago when they got down on their knees and begged the Canadian government to spend all its energy and resources in order to develop this product for United States consumption. Now, having found uranium in their own country, are they going to do what they have done with other base metals, namely turn off the tap when they find a tap of their own?
The United States government did have a responsibility in this matter. It was as a result of United States government-I was going to say pleas-requests that we developed this uranium industry in the country for the common defence of the west. Immediately after that development occurred and when it was clear that there was going to be a great source of uranium supply in Canada the government of that country made the same kind of effort in the United States to find and develop uranium. Having regard to the contract they made with Canada and having regard to the moral obligation which I claim they had to keep this industry a thriving one in Canada, it seems to me the least the United States authorities could have done at that time, having found uranium, was to use that uranium as a reserve and not allow the production in that country at that time to interfere with or destroy the uranium industry in Canada. If defence co-operation means anything-and I have said this in the house and outside the house-it means the coordination of defence industry. For the United States to have encouraged Canada to develop this kind of defence product because it was necessary for our common defence and then to cut off the contract as they did last autumn was not in my view an exhibition of what they often talk about down there, integrated continental defence.
Naturally that was the time for the Canadian government to bring political pressure to bear on the United States government to get this situation straightened out. That is why I brought up the matter again in the house on April 23, 1959, as reported at page 2971 of Hansard. I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce what progress was being made in this matter and whether anything was being done, but the minister was

not very worried at that time because his reply to me was as follows:
There is plenty of opportunity for discussion during the course of this year with regard to those options-
I point out that this was April 23, 1959, not very long before we got the news last autumn that the options were not going to be taken up. The minister went on to say:
-and there will be plenty of time to discuss- if the information can be obtained-the requirements for the period 1962 to 1966.
The minister continued:
The picture is not as gloomy as the Leader of the Opposition attempted to show in his speech the other night, or as he is perhaps attempting to convey by means of this question.
Subsequent events showed beyond any shadow of doubt that the picture was even gloomier than I portrayed it to be at that time, yet since that time we have had no information from any member of this government as to what political steps were taken and on what level to get the United States to take a reasonable view of this situation.
The question came up again in this house on June 25, 1959. We were then approaching the zero hour when the options were to be turned down. On that occasion, as reported at page 5178 of Hansard, I had this to say:
The minister has been to Washington to discuss this matter with the United States government. He spent a day there a couple of months ago, I think, but I suggest to him that the importance of this matter justifies the most formal and the most impressive representations that can be made to the United States government at the highest possible level.
Further along in my statement I repeated that thought when I said:
I hope that not only will the government give this matter the attention it deserves on the highest diplomatic level but that before long it will be able to make an announcement that a specific arrangement has been made with the United States. If continental defence means anything at all- and, of course, it does mean something-it means that some consideration has to be given to the economic and industrial aspects of defence on a continental basis as well as to the strategic aspect and if there was ever an important economic and industrial aspect of defence it is the supply of uranium for defence purposes.
What did we get as a result of this intervention?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. In what way would the hon. gentleman use this material strictly for defence purposes?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
That is not a very difficult question to answer, because the minister knows probably better than I do that unfortunately, because of the state of the world in which we live, perhaps 94 per cent, 95 per cent, or more of this material is going
Crisis in Uranium Industry into defence equipment in the United States at the present time. That is how it is being used, for defence purposes. It is going into different nuclear weapons, defensive tactical nuclear weapons of the United States, which my hon. friend and his colleagues have decided they will use in defence equipment for the Canadian forces, and surely that is an answer to his question.
On July 14, not discouraged, I brought the matter up again, and the minister had this to say, as reported at page 5957 of Hansard:
The matter is under consideration, and we have had discussions with the authorities in the United States, but they have indicated that there is some uncertainty with regard to their requirement after 1962.
Then, he added this:
However, I do not think there is cause for alarm over this matter at the present time.
There was cause for alarm over this matter at that time, as we learned later in the year when, as the result of discussions of some kind that went on in Washington with the United States authorities, there was an announcement that there was to be a stretch-out of the contract, but no new purchases of uranium were to be made outside this contract. This was done presumably after negotiations with the United States. I should like to ask the minister, whenever he gets the opportunity, to reply to these questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: That is up to you.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Another 10 minutes.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Did the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) take part in those negotiations? Were those political and defence considerations bearing on this contract and those options brought to the attention of the United States government? Was that done by a minister of the government? Was it done by the Secretary of State for External Affairs? Did the Prime Minister ever bring up this matter with the head of the United States government? The answer must be no because we have asked the Prime Minister more than once and he has not been able to reply to the questions. How were these negotiations conducted which dealt with such a vital raw material, strategical and economical as this one was? Was the government at that time-November, I think-satisfied? Indeed, the press communique said they were satisfied with the stretch-out arrangement which did not result in the purchase of an extra pound of uranium from this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
To make more nuclear bombs.

Crisis in Uranium Industry

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Is my hon. friend suggesting now the reason no pressure was brought to bear on the United States to pick up those options was that uranium was going into defence equipment for the United States forces, for Canadian forces and for NATO forces, because that is the implication of his reply; that he did not care very much about the idea of this material going into nuclear bombs?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: You are advocating the building of more nuclear bombs?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: This is a new reason, and it will be of very great interest to this country that a government which has not advocated the unilateral destruction or abolition of nuclear weapons, which belongs to a coalition where nuclear weapons are being used, which has a continental defence arrangement with the United States which relies for its deterrent value on nuclear bombs, now has said, we did not try too hard to get those contracts renewed because we were worried about this material going into nuclear weapons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Such a distortion.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I ask the minister to correct that now. If that is not the minister's position he can rise in his place and say so because it was the minister and not I who raised this question of this material going into nuclear bombs, and asked me whether I agreed with that. I ask the minister something else. During those negotiations in Washington which resulted in this stretch-out arrangement which has been received with such satisfaction-my moral friends to my left are making observations about the use of a material for defence purposes which the Canadian forces are using, but which they do not wish to make available to the United States, which is making the defence equipment which our forces are using. That, Mr. Speaker, is the most illogical, hypocritical attitude that anyone can take in regard to this matter. If that is their position they should have cut off the supply of uranium as soon as they came into office and should have seen that none of it went into bombs. They did not do that until two or three years after, when the United States refused to buy it any longer,
I will ask another question of the minister. In those negotiations in Washington, which resulted in this stretch-out arrangement which, according to the minister's statement at the time, was a very satisfactory solution to this problem but has not been considered to be very satisfactory by anybody else, was the uranium industry of this country consulted? Did they take any part in the negotiations? I ask him whether the arrangements that were put to the United
[Mr. Churchill.I
States were submitted in any way to the representatives of industry? Were they consulted in any way? Were they allowed to give their views as to this stretch-out arrangement before it was concluded with the United States? The answers to these questions would seem to me to be a pretty obvious negative, if one can judge from the statement made by Dr. D. R. Derry, vice president of Rio Tinto Mining Company, in Toronto on January 13, to the conference on uranium and atomic energy called by the provincial government of Ontario. At that conference Dr. Derry read a paper which included this paragraph:
The simultaneous announcement in Ottawa and Washington on November 6 that the United States would not exercise the options they held on Canadian uranium production in the years 1962 to 1966, came as a severe blow to the Canadian producers. This was particularly so because the government, doubtless for what they considered to be the best of reasons, had not kept the producers informed about their negotiations with the United States until the final decision was reached. The industry did expect a partial exercise of the options which would have enabled a smoother transition to the period of healthier demand which is hoped and expected towards the end of the 1960's and early 1970's.
So far as this statement is concerned, it is quite clear-and perhaps the minister will deny its accuracy, if it is not accurate-that the industry was not consulted about those negotiations, about this arrangement, which had such a vital effect on its future and on the future of the people who are working in this industry until the agreement had been reached with the United States government. After that, consultation, of course, would be useless.
That is the situation. What is the government doing about it? On February 5 the minister said in the house, and I am quoting from page 772 of Hansard:
But let me say that I have every sympathy, and that the government has every sympathy, with those concerned with the situation at Elliot Lake, and that steps are being taken to make sure that the people there will not suffer unduly from the changes that are taking place in the uranium industry.
The minister repeated that assurance on the air on February 21, last Sunday, when he said:
Over the next two or three years there will be a reduction in employment in these areas. This is very unfortunate but my hope is that as mining development goes on in Canada in other forms there will be plenty of opportunity for employment for those who may be displaced in the uranium mines.
What have we learned today about the possibility of those miners being used in other mines in Canada? We learn today from reports in the press that miners are being brought in from Europe-and they cannot get in here without the approval and permission

of the government-at a time when the minister said that miners who may be out of work in Elliot Lake will have a chance, he hopes, to find work in other mines. So I ask the minister, what is he actually doing to carry out this promise? What steps are being taken to make sure that the people there will not suffer unduly?
We on this side have asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) more than once whether he would make sure that the severance pay to be given by the companies to the 3,500 miners who will be unemployed shortly will not be considered as income for income tax purposes, and the best we can get out of the Minister of Labour on this point is that it is expected that the unemployment insurance advisory committee will meet on March 4, I think. That does not show the sense of urgency which is required to deal with this matter.
I ask the minister-we have asked him already in the house-and the Prime Minister whether they will go to Elliot Lake and see the situation there and also to any other uranium area affected. Elliot Lake, of course, because of the size of the community and the number of people affected is going to suffer much more than any other area. The minister has not yet been able to visit there and see for himself what is going on. The Prime Minister-incidentally, he said the other day that he had been at Elliot Lake which will be a very great surprise to the people there-has other duties, of course, and he has not been able to visit the place. But I hope the minister will find an opportunity shortly to visit Elliot Lake and see on the spot what can be done to carry out his promise to make sure that the people there will not suffer unduly from the changes that are taking place.
What can be done? What can be done to help this and other communities affected but particularly this community which is going to be the most affected because it is much the largest? What can be done to help in terms of providing new activity and providing industry and employment for the Elliot Lake-Blind River area which at the present time depends exclusively on this one product for its livelihood? What can be done? Can pressure on the highest political level he brought to bear on the United States government to reconsider its position in this matter? That does not seem to be possible so far as the government is concerned according to the communique which resulted from this happy conference held in Washington last week at which we were told everything went off beautifully and with respect to which the press tells us that everything
Crisis in Uranium Industry was all sweetness and light and people admired each other and there were no problems except ones that were bilateral and nothing could be done about them. In this communique we have the following paragraph:
Canadian and United States of America representatives discussed the outlook of the uranium industry in both countries and agreed on the importance of keeping each other informed of development prospects.
It is not development prospects that we are so worried about at the present time in the uranium industry in Canada; it is the salvation of the industry and the livelihood of the people who are affected by it.
There is another aspect of this question which should be mentioned in terms of what might or could be done to help the situation. We now have a government crown company, Eldorado, a very efficient company, well run, well administered, which has played a very helpful part in the development of this industry in Canada in the past. It is a crown company; it is the agency for marketing all uranium produced in Canada. All uranium from private corporations has to be marketed through this crown company. Therefore it is the sole marketing agency. It is at the same time a producer in an industry where the private companies are not all going to be able to survive. That is obvious now because some have already been incorporated in others. I ask the minister whether he thinks in these special circumstances, these emergency circumstances, it is a desirable thing to keep the crown company in production at the expense of private companies going out of production. Perhaps he will be able to indicate the views of the government on that score.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Would the Leader of the Opposition answer a question on that point? He would then suggest that Uranium City disappear and other places be sustained, because Uranium City is maintained by the employment offered by the Eldorado mine.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: I am not suggesting that any city disappear. I am suggesting that every step that can be taken be taken to maintain this industry on the best possible basis. I am asking my hon. friend, and this he will be able to refer to, whether in these circumstances-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: If you give him time.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: The minister will have lots of time during this session to talk about uranium.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
You are certainly seeing to it that he has as little as possible tonight.

Crisis in Uranium Industry

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: The Minister oi Finance (Mr. Fleming), as I said before, should be the last man to talk about somebody being kept out of the discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: It is a contemptible trick. You ought to be ashamed of yourself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: I should like to remind my hon. friend who has interrupted that there was no whining on our part when these tactics were adopted by members of the government party when they were in opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: It was never done before by a leader of the opposition.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: We have never had a minister of finance so ill-tempered before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: It is a contemptible trick.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: I should like to give the minister some time to reply but if my hon. friend keeps on interrupting that will take up a lot of time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Shallow hypocrisy.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: You are the hypocrite.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: There is a second suggestion I should like to make to the minister. Has the government given consideration to the establishment in this country of a plant for the production of enriched uranium? It must be clear to the minister and the government that in the future the material which will be of greatest importance in this industry will not be raw but enriched uranium.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Not necessarily.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
There is a good deal of evidence to support that view. As a result the United States may very well get control of the uranium export industry in the world because of two things. It is the only country that now manufactures enriched uranium. It is the only country which is now making reactors available to other countries which reactors can only use enriched uranium. Canada is in a very fortunate position so far as the production of enriched uranium is concerned because we have abundant quantities of water power which is essential for this operation.
It might well have been considered economically impossible to do this a few years ago because of the cost involved, but I am sure my hon. friend has read a pamphlet by an authority on this matter, Dr. John Davis, dated November 18, 1959, entitled, "The Case for a Uranium Enrichment Plant in Canada", in which he points out among


a lot of other things that the cost of an enriched uranium plant now is much less than it was, much less indeed than when the United States built their plant. He thought that it could be done for $200 million and he even got down to $100 million for a particular type of plant. But let us say $200 million whereas it cost the Americans between $500 million and $600 million to build each plant; so a plant built in Canada at a cost of $200 million, a most modern plant, would surely put our industry in a position to compete with United States enriched uranium in the markets of the world.
This might be a very important development to save the uranium industry of Canada during this difficult period of transition until uranium is required for peaceful purposes in quantities that will consume all our uranium, and that is going to be some years.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: That development figure should be $500 million.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I am quoting figures given by a man who has made a very careful investigation. If it will cost $500 million no doubt the minister will be able to substantiate that.
Then, of course, there is the question of the construction of a nuclear power station. The government has agreed to build a second one at Kincardine and perhaps the time will come when a third will be required.
Then there is the question of the nuclear research station that is now to be built in Manitoba. Other things being equal, Mr. Speaker, there would be no one on this side who would question the choice of location by the government for a particular nuclear research station. When this matter came up some months ago there was no controversy over it. Everybody in the house hoped to get the nuclear research station for his own constituency and I put in a bid for Elliot Lake because I thought it had some of the facilities that were required.
But since that decision was made the situation has changed very greatly. We will now perhaps have in Elliot Lake facilities and services available for this kind of development which will have to be built at very great expense in any other area of Canada that may be chosen for this station. I have just said the provincial and federal governments spent between $50 and $70 million at Elliot Lake in the provision of services and facilities. It would seem to be good economy to save that money if the station could be built in another area and if, at the same time by putting it there, this community could also be saved. That is the only reason why anyone would ask the government to reconsider the decision which has been made.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: What have you got against Manitoba?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Nobody has got anything against any part of Canada. I have just said that if other things were equal Manitoba would be a desirable place in every respect for this station. I am asking the minister if he considers, in the light of developments since last October, whether things are still equal. No doubt, he will tell us that in due course.
The minister now says that the decision was made-he said this in his broadcast the other night, and I will read what he said so I will not be misquoting him:
A suggestion has been put forward that the proposed nuclear research establishment be put in at Elliot Lake.
Then, he went on:
Acting on the advice of the directors of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, who made a careful survey of the situation across Canada, the government decided that the nuclear research establishment should be located at Whiteshell in Manitoba.
According to the minister now the site was chosen by Atomic Energy of Canada. However, last October, when he announced that this station was to be established in Manitoba he said, speaking in Winnipeg, according to the Winnipeg Free Press of October 1, 1959:
Manitoba was elected for the site, the trade minister said, because the province, with the exception of military and agricultural research centres, had little in the form of industrial research. He said Manitoba had no particular physical advantages that led to its selection for the next research centre.
There is quite a contradiction between those two reasons given. Indeed the reply to the minister's most recent reason for establishing the centre in Manitoba was given by the men in the uranium industry themselves, who have pointed out in a statement that there was no technical reason why the station should not be at Elliot Lake. The president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited himself, whose company the minister says was responsible for the choice of this site, had this to say as quoted in the Sudbury Star of January 26, 1960:
J. Lome Gray, president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, told the Star that from a technological standpoint he could see no valid reason why the new establishment could not be located at Elliot lake. He said government reasons for wishing to locate it in Manitoba should emanate from the government.
That is sufficient to answer what the minister said the other night over the air. The minister also said that plans are too far advanced now to change them, even if it were desirable to change them. But he spoke very differently about that last autumn when he said that it would be a long time before
Crisis in Uranium Industry construction would begin and before plans would be ready for construction. The secretary of Atomic Energy of Canada has said that nothing has yet been designed and it will be a year before the plans are ready. So, I ask the minister if he will inform the house whether any considerations have now been advanced, because of the situation of the industry, which in his view necessitate a reconsideration of this matter by the government. It was only in these circumstances of emergency that anyone on this side suggested any such reconsideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Would the hon. member suggest the transfer of the nuclear station to Uranium City?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The minister has asked
whether I would suggest the transfer to Uranium City. Surely the minister knows that if we are trying to save a community and all the people involved in that community it is more important to save a large community than a smaller community. While everybody has every sympathy for the people of Uranium City who are going to suffer from this situation, the minister will probably agree with me if I tell him there are, say, 3,000 in Uranium City?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: There are 8,000.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
There are between 25,000 and
30,000	in Elliot Lake and Blind River, and that is a community in which much more money has been spent-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: You did not put any money into Uranium City.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
-and in which more homes have been established by people who expected to stay there. Therefore, if you have to make a choice, and I hope you will not have to do so, surely the minister, if he were reconsidering that matter, would consider it more important to move the research centre to the larger centre rather than the smaller centre which is very remote from those institutions which the minister himself has told us are very important to have nearby and which was one of the reasons he said they adopted this Manitoba site.
In closing, I would just remind the minister-that he will have 20 minutes to answer some of these questions-that at page 772 of Hansard for February 5, 1960 he said, and I ask him to explain this in the light of what has happened since, that steps are being taken to make sure that the people there will not suffer unduly-he is talking about Elliot Lake-from the changes that are taking place in the uranium industry.

Crisis in Uranium. Industry

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: I assume that the minister wishes to speak on the grievance raised by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
That is true, Mr. Speaker. He has asked some questions and he has very kindly offered to give me 20 minutes when he spoke for 55 minutes in order to deal with this very important problem.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) started off with a review of the developments of the uranium industry in Canada, and then passed on to some other topics. The development of the uranium industry in Canada has been a spectacular development, and up until 1953 there was a serious shortage of uranium. There was the necessity, on the part of the western allies, to find more uranium in order to build weapons because of the failure, in 1947, of the plan to discontinue making nuclear weapons and because of the developments in Russia in this particular field. It was, therefore, a matter of self-preservation in various countries of the world, not only the United States but Canada as well, to launch out in search of uranium in order that there would be an assured supply for military purposes. This was done and great discoveries were made, none greater than the discovery in the Blind River area.
The United States authorities urged the Canadians to do what they could in this expansion. I do not think that they begged us or that we made any tremendous sacrifice in order to do this because the amount of money that was made available was substantial and provided quite an incentive. At any rate, the steps were taken and the exploration was successful. Uranium deposits were found in Canada. I do not doubt that, in 1953, they were the largest and most important in the world. But at the same time, other countries were actively engaged in this business.
May I direct the attention of the Leader of the Opposition to the situation as it prevailed in September of 1954. The late Mr. R. J. Henry, who was then vice president of Eldorado Mining and Refining Company, spoke to the provincial ministers of mines in Winnipeg in September, 1954, and he said this:
Canada is not the only producer of uranium, as you are well aware. Production in the United States reached record levels this year-
That is 1954.
At least 15 orebodies are known to contain reserves in excess of 100,000 tons each and several of these greatly exceed this figure and the ore is high grade. By the year-end, nine mills will be producing on the Colorado plateau and mills in other areas are under construction or planned. Uranium is also being recovered as a by-product

from four phosphate plants in Florida, and negotiations with several others for additional facilities are in progress. In South Africa six plants are in operation, and several others are scheduled for completion this year. South Africa's potential for low cost uranium is very great. In Australia two plants will be in operation this year. By this you can see we are going to have plenty of competition in a world market.
Not only was there evidence of competition in a world market but there was evidence that uranium was coming into considerable supply that might exceed demand and my hon. friends were in office at that time in
1954.	In the succeeding years of 1955 and 1956 contracts were entered into with the United States authorities for the production of uranium in Canada and they were very substantial contracts. Those contracts were entered into by the United States atomic energy commission with Eldorado, the government purchasing agency in Canada and then with the producing mines. These contracts ran for five years and they did get in the contracts an option clause which could be taken up in March, 1961.
My hon. friend might be interested in what the then minister of trade and commerce in
1955,	Mr. Howe, said with regard to some of these matters. He indicated that these contracts would be written or available not later than March 31, 1956 and the mines had to come into production not later than April 1, 1957. He was asked questions about supply and demand. He said this, and I quote his words from a press release which was issued on August 3, 1955:
As I indicated in the House of Commons recently, there is no information at this time as to whether the military demand will continue beyond March 31, 1962. If the military requirement should be extended beyond March 31, 1962, the government's decision as to its future purchasing policy will be announced.
There was no clear understanding that this thing was going to go on indefinitely. In 1954 it was known to the government and to the industry that there was a growing world supply of uranium. The contracts were written for a five-year period. My hon. friend says, "Well, we did not want to tie up the uranium in this country for a longer period". It would have been sound common sense to have contracts extending longer than five years when it was evident that other countries were in the production field with regard to uranium.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: You took the other view then.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Don't interrupt.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend talked about this dangerous scarcity. The dangerous scarcity evaporated when these discoveries were made and there was really no reason for

the United States authorities to consider relying solely upon Canadian resources. It was only prudent for them to undertake their own exploration program and that also was a very successful program. When their uranium mines were found and when they came into production they were satisfied that they had a balanced program that assured a supply of uranium in their own country for most of their military needs, and the contracts they had with Canada, South Africa, Australia and the Belgian Congo gave them other sources of supply.
My hon. friend talks about the United States not living up to its moral obligation to take up the options to have more uranium available, as he describes it. Available for what? For a stockpile? If so, a stockpile of what? A stockpile of uranium weapons so that we will ensure that the world will be completely blown up when the time comes that somebody is foolish enough to set these things off? Actually what my hon. friend is suggesting, when he says that we failed to press the United States to take up these options, is that we took no action at all.
What action did he take in 1956? In 1956, when my hon. friend was secretary of state for external affairs, this situation with regard to uranium production was very well known to the then government and to the world.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: And to the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: But did my hon. friend take any action then to see whether or not these options were going to be taken up? Not one single thing did he do as secretary of state for external affairs. He had from then until a date in June, 1957 which is well remembered in this country. Did he take any action up to that June 10?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: -or June 21, 1957? Not a bit of action did he take.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: That was the first year of the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: His interest in uranium in his own constituency has just developed in 1959 and it is only then that he started asking questions.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: After you destroyed the industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: With regard to the contracts and the options, the time to have taken action was in 1956 and 1957 when world production was steadily increasing and the Americans were expanding exploration and their production in North America.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Will the minister permit a question?
Crisis in Uranium Industry

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Does he realize that the time of which he speaks is the time at which most of these mines were starting to come into production and before there were many of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Starting over-production which your government encouraged.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: My point is that in 1954, 1955, 1956 and 1957 world production of uranium was on the increase. My hon. friends should have known these facts but they did not know them and they are responsible for the overexpansion of the uranium industry and the contraction of time to five years which should have been expanded to at least ten years because you cannot conduct mining operations on a five-year basis and put in established communities with any chance for their survival. If you have a ten-year period or twenty-year period there is a possibility then of having an established community set up. But my hon. friends, working on the slender thread of five-year contracts, misled the people who are now living in Elliot Lake. A miner of Elliot Lake, when he appeared on a television program on Sunday said, "Why did not somebody tell us?" These are the people who should have told them in 1957.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: They knew it or they should have known it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Why did they not say, "This is a temporary occupation for you; this is all we can guarantee with regard to your occupation here at these mines because the options have not been taken up and during our term of office as a Liberal government we took no action to have the options taken up in 1956 and 1957".

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Before the contract was
signed? How do you take up an option before the contract is signed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: But no; they misled the people terribly. I certainly sympathize with the people of Elliot Lake.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: What are you going to do for them?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Don't interrupt.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Just give me time to finish.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: What are you going to do for them?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: I just have a few minutes left.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The minister has limited time available and I would hope hon. members might hear him.

Crisis in Uranium, Industry

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: That is only lair.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: My hon. friend attempted to make out that the government took no action. We did consult with the authorities in the United States.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: One day in Washington.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
We saved the uranium industry in Canada from complete collapse in 1962. That is what faced it in 1962 had we not made the arrangement with the United States for this stretch-out program, a basic contract written between Eldorado and the United States authorities covering the entire production that had been bargained for from the Canadian mines and that became a firm settlement.
Had that not been done, what would have happened? The contract would have been lost and the export of uranium would have declined very seriously. But we arranged with the United States authorities a stretch-out program under this master contract and saved the uranium situation in Canada to the extent of $120 million. My hon. friend says nothing about that, and that is why I said on November 8 that it was a successful termination of our negotiations with the United States. The sum of $120 million went into the uranium industry and provides employment over several years which would not have been provided had we not made that arrangement.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: A successful operation but the patient died.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend asked, what about pressure on the United States? He said, cannot we bring political pressure on the United States at this stage? I ask, for what purpose? They have announced that their military requirements have been met. They are stockpiling and have stockpiled uranium for military purposes. The peacetime uses of uranium have not advanced to the stage where they require imports from Canada, so what is the political pressure we are to exert on the United States at this time? Can we go to them and say, "We have a uranium industry in Canada; take more from us for the next five, six, or ten years"? For what purpose? For the peaceful uses of uranium? No, because the peaceful uses of uranium have not advanced to the stage where much in the way of poundage is required. Are we to press the United States to get more uranium from Canada in order to make more thermonuclear bombs when they say they have a surplus? I do not know what attitude the Nobel Foundation would take to that suggestion.
My hon. friend has suggested that the Eldorado mine be closed down. He says that

the people of Uranium City are not as important as the people of Elliot Lake.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, the minister knows perfectly well, and if he was not so heated he would realize it, that I made no such statement at any time, as Hansard will show. It is a good thing it is nearly ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
My hon. friend said that
24,000	people are more important than 8,000 people. That is recorded in Hansard and I state it again to make sure it is there.
Then he talked about building an enriched uranium plant, and his evidence was founded on a report made by a Mr. Davis. Again, I have not time to bring forward the evidence here, but you have to build a plant and develop the electricity, and these diffusion plants need enormous quantities of electricity. To develop the electricity and build the plant, an estimated $500 million, according to the experts who are as knowledgeable as Mr. Davis in this field, is required. The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the nuclear power station at Kincardine and hoped that this would be built soon. Let us not forget the fact that Ontario has not fared too badly with regard to atomic research and nuclear development. There is the NRX reactor at Chalk River as well as the NRU. NPD is being developed which, in the course of the next twelve months, will put 20,000 kilowatts of energy into the Ontario grid. The CANDU station near Kincardine at a cost of $60 million is being developed within the next few years to put 200,000 kilowatts into the Ontario grid.
That is a substantial contribution to atomic research in this country and is a substantial contribution by this province in the nuclear research field. I think this government's policy has been to spread out the advantages right across this country, and to establish a nuclear research establishment elsewhere sounds reasonable to most people except the Leader of the Opposition. Other reactors which may be built in the future will have to go to various sections of this country which are power deficient, and some of those are not in this area; yet there may be other reactors established in Ontario. I would like to see more of them. Again it will be the peaceful use of uranium for which they will be required.
Now with regard to Elliot Lake. I hope to make a visit to Elliot Lake, and I am also going to Uranium City. These people have been upset, and naturally upset, and provision will have to be made for them. But let us view the situation carefully, Mr. Speaker.

Of the 24,000 or 25,000 people at Elliot Lake, I think half of the employed miners are single men, 4,500 of them living in bunkhouses and some hundreds more living in trailers. It is not exactly a permanent situation. However, what we will do there with the cooperation of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) who is responsible for national housing is that we will see that the people there are not inconvenienced due to the necessity of having to shift from one place to another. And on the industry itself must rest a great responsibility to see that employees are not let out just overnight.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext: Like Avro.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO MAINTAIN URANIUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I have talked to the leaders of the industry and suggested to them that they must cushion this blow and make it possible for these people who have worked for them for years to transfer to other occupations without too great an inconvenience. These are things which we intend to do with the co-operation of the provincial government and the companies themselves, to help cushion this blow to the uranium industry. It is not the only industry which has had to make adjustments and I think this can be done over a period of years. I do not see Elliot Lake becoming a ghost town; far from it. The number of permanent dwellings there will support a town of between 8,000 to
10,000	people. There may be a contraction, but the major producing mines are still there, still operating, and will operate for another three years, and then there will be a decline in production. By that time there may be an increased demand for the peaceful use of uranium.
Just to give a rapid forecast of that, it looks as if uranium is now in greater supply than demand. By 1965 supply and demand come a bit closer together, and by 1970 it is expected by people who are experts in this field that world supply will be just under the projected world demand. I grant that there is an awkward little period in there where we are not sure at this moment what the future for uranium is, but by 1963 or 1964 we will have a much clearer idea.
Canada's atomic research efforts in the use of natural uranium and heavy water will by that time have reached the stage where we can determine if it is economically successful, and if it is there may be an export possibility for Canada of that type of reactor based on the use of natural uranium.

The duties of a classification officer may be briefly summed up as follows: Preparation of case histories of inmates; assessment, selection, and counselling of inmates in various phases of rehabilitative treatment; presentation of all pertinent data to the classification board (treatment team); participation in the implementation and subsequent appraisal and readjustment of the treatment plan decided upon in respect of each inmate.

Mr. S. F. Rae,
Minister,
Canadian Embassy,
Washington, D.C.
Dear Mr. Rae:
With reference to your letter of this date in which you request assurance that, in the event S-3019 is enacted into law, the department of state will recommend to the President that Canadian vessels operating primarily on the great lakes and St. Lawrence river which make occasional trips to the Canadian maritime provinces in the Canadian coastal trade be excluded from the designation of foreign vessels under section 3 (a) of the said bill, I take pleasure in stating that the department will make such a recommendation.
Sincerely yours,
Ivan B. White
February 19, 1960
Mr. Ivan B. White,
Department of State,
Washington, D.C.
Dear Mr. White,
The agreement of the Canadian government which is transmitted concurrently herewith to the terms of the aide memoire in regard to the bill on great lakes pilotage is subject to the following reservation. Section 9 (c) of the bill does not fully meet the Canadian requirements in that lake vessels which occasionally operate through the St. Lawrence to the maritime provinces in the Canadian coastal trade are not covered. The Canadian government considers that these vessels should be covered and understands that United States officials concerned with this matter are sympathetic to the Canadian position.
During discussions between the appropriate officials of our two governments, United States officials indicated that the position of such vessels could be protected under section 3 (a) by not being designated pursuant to the section.
We would appreciate receiving assurance that in the event S-3019 is enacted into law, the department of state will recommend to the President that Canadian vessels operating primarily on the great lakes and St. Lawrence river which make occasional trips to the Canadian maritime provinces in the Canadian coastal trade be excluded from the
designation of foreign vessels to be made by the President under section 3 (a) of the said bill.
Yours sincerely,
S. F. Rae
Aide Memoire
In discussions of great lakes pilotage between United States and Canadian officials following the receipt of the Canadian aide memoire of September 11, 1959, the Canadian officials were informed of the provisions of a proposed draft bill on the subject which was prepared by representatives of interested agencies of the government of the United States. The principal purposes of the proposed bill would be to establish certain pilotage requirements for the navigation of United States waters of great lakes and St. Lawrence river by vessels operating on ocean routes to and from great lakes, and to provide a basis for a regulated system of pilotage to meet those requirements.
Provision is made for co-ordination of this pilotage system with a Canadian system on the basis of reciprocal recognition of and equitable participation by United States and Canadian pilots in the pilotage of the vessels to which the bill would be applicable. These pilots would be registered by an appropriate agency of their respective countries, and vessels to which the bill is applicable would be required to have registered pilots in their service for the navigation of designated United States waters. It is the understanding of the United States government that Canadian waters will also be designated in which the services of registered pilots will be required.
In undesignated waters of great lakes, the vessels to which the proposed bill would be applicable would be required to have on board either a registered pilot or an officer of their regular complement who would be qualified for the navigation of the undesignated waters and licensed either by United States coastguard or the appropriate agency of Canada.
As a result of the above-mentioned discussions, the Canadian representatives indicated that their government would be prepared to recommend to parliament that legislation be adopted permitting coordination on the above indicated basis, if United States enacted legislation along the lines of the proposed draft bill. It is the United States government's understanding that provision would be made to restrict the registration of Canadian pilots

to persons, other than members of the regular complement of a vessel, who hold a master's certificate or equivalent licence, unlimited as to tonnage, issued by the Department of Transport to authorize navigation of great lakes and pilotage services on routes specified therein.
The term "equivalent licence" as used in the proposed United States draft bill means a licence issued to a St. Lawrence river pilot to authorize the navigation of those portions of the river specified therein. In this connection Canadian officials explained that St. Lawrence river pilots are specially trained for pilotage in the districts for which they are licensed, and that they are not required to obtain a master's certificate, although some do hold such a certificate. Under the proposed co-ordinated arrangements, Canada would register the holder of a St. Lawrence river pilot's licence solely for pilotage service on that river.
The Canadian officials further indicated that the Canadian government would include in any proposed legislation such provisions as might be considered necessary to authorize the Department of Transport to issue certificates qualifying for the navigation of the "open" (i.e. undesignated) waters of great lakes those officers of the regular complements of ocean vessels who meet the following requirements:
(1)	Hold an appropriate certificate of competency as master, valid for voyages in any part of the world and issued or recognized by the country in which the ship is registered.
(2)	Have the experience of at least two round trips, within the preceding two years, in the "open" or undesignated waters of great lakes where the vessel will be operating.
(3)	Possess a working knowledge of great lakes rules of the road as evidenced by exam.
(4)	Have proficiency in the English language, to be tested also by exam, sufficient
to make effective use of the radiotelephone.
(5)	Have knowledge of the practice of following separate upbound and downbound courses on great lakes, giving due regard to the suitability of such courses for deep draft vessels.
The substance of the proposed draft bill which was the subject of the above-mentioned discussions is now embodied in a bill introduced in the Senate as S 3019. The government of the United States of America would appreciate being informed as to the accuracy and applicability of the foregoing understanding of the intentions of the Canadian government with respect to S 3019.
The State Department,
Washington, D.C.,
February 19, 1960.
Canadian Reply
Aide Memoire
An aide memoire presented to the Canadian embassy in Washington by the department of state on February 19 outlines the manner in which Canadian and United States legislation aimed at establishing certain pilotage requirements for the navigation of the waters of the great lakes and St. Lawrence river could be co-ordinated if the legislative proposals contained in a bill known as S 3019 are approved by the United States congress. In the event that that bill does become law in the United States, it is the intention of the Canadian government to submit to the Canadian parliament legislative proposals which would effect just such a co-ordinated pilotage regime in the great lakes in the manner indicated in the United States aide memoire.
Canadian Embassy,
Washington, D.C.,
February 19, I960.
